title: Hollow Butterfly Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: per-cell wing-and-edge checks versus building one hollow wing directly and reusing it on both sides, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a butterfly shape with 2n minus 1 rows, where each of the two wings is hollow, only its own two edges are stars, growing toward each other until they meet at the widest row, then shrinking apart again.

blocks.title: Analogy: Butterfly Wings Made of Wire
blocks.text: This is the same butterfly seen earlier, except every wing is now only its outline, bent from thin wire rather than filled in solid. Each wing still grows and shrinks exactly as before, but only its outer tip and its inner edge, closest to the body, are ever solid, everything between them is open space.

blocks.caption: Each wing is hollow, only its outer tip and its inner edge are stars

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 1","*      *","m is 1, each wing is a single star, too narrow to hollow out, separated by the largest gap, 6."],["Row 2","**    **","m is 2, each wing is 2 stars with no room for an interior, separated by a gap of 4."],["Row 3","* *  * *","m is 3, each wing is now wide enough to hollow out, a star, one hollow space, a star."],["Row 4","*  **  *","m is 4, the widest row, each wing is a star, two hollow spaces, a star, and the two wings now sit directly next to each other with no gap."],["Row 5","* *  * *","m is 3 again, measured from the bottom tip, matching row 3."],["Row 6","**    **","m is 2, narrowing back toward the bottom tip."],["Row 7","*      *","m is 1, the final row, matching row 1."]]}

blocks.text: With n = 1, both wings collapse into a single touching star, too narrow to hollow out.
No rows at all, so nothing is printed.
This shape looks unfamiliar, but it is worth checking how much of it decomposes directly into ideas already used earlier in this division.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The distance measurement, m equal to min of r and 2n minus r, and the fixed total row width, 2n, are exactly the same ideas already used for the solid butterfly.

Observation 2: What changes is that each wing is now hollow, only its outer tip and its inner edge are stars, exactly the same edge only construction already used for the hollow pyramid's ordinary rows, just applied to a wing instead of a full triangle side.

Observation 3: Testing a small example, n equal to 4, shows the left wing and the right wing are always exactly the same string, for any given row, since both are built from the exact same m.

Observation 4: That means there is no need to construct the right wing separately at all, building one hollow wing string once and reusing it directly on both sides of the gap produces the correct row.
Recognizing that the two halves of a row are literally identical, not just similarly shaped, is what turns "build two hollow wings" into "build one hollow wing and place it twice".

For every row, first work out its distance from the nearer tip, then check every one of the 2n columns individually, deciding whether that position falls inside the left wing, the right wing, or the gap between them, and for either wing, whether it lands on that wing's own edge.

items: Loop over every row r, from 1 to 2n minus 1.
Compute m, the distance of this row from whichever tip is closer.
Check every one of the 2n columns for this row.
If the column falls inside the left wing, print a star only at its first or last position, a space otherwise.
If the column falls inside the right wing, apply the same edge only rule to that wing.
Otherwise print a space, the gap between the two wings.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: find the distance from the nearest tip, then check wing membership and edge position

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: m is computed once per row exactly as with the solid butterfly, folding both the widening and narrowing halves into one shared distance value.

The edge check, k equal to 0 or k equal to m minus 1, is applied separately inside both the left wing branch and the right wing branch, even though the two wings are always built from the exact same m and therefore always produce the exact same shape.
The inner loop still checks each of the 2n columns one at a time, printing a single character per iteration, which is exactly the inefficiency the optimized version removes.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every column in every row is checked against wing membership and, within a wing, against the edge condition, before deciding what to print.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since every row checks a fixed 2n columns and there are proportional to n such rows.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: once the wing size m for a row is known, checking every position inside each wing individually adds nothing, since only the first and last position of a wing ever hold a star. The entire hollow wing shape can instead be built directly in one operation, and reused for both sides, since the two wings are always identical to each other.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: the same edge check is derived independently for the left wing and again for the right wing, even though both wings always share the exact same m and therefore the exact same shape.

What stays the same as two earlier problems: the distance measurement and fixed total width from the butterfly, and the hollow edge only construction from the hollow pyramid.

What is genuinely new here: since both wings are always identical, building the hollow wing string a single time and placing it on both sides removes the duplicated construction entirely, not just the duplicated per column checking.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, a star, a gap of spaces, and a star, or just a single star when m is 1 or 2, builds the one hollow wing needed.

The core idea: compute m once per row, build a single hollow wing string from it, then reuse that same string on both sides of the gap.

For each row, compute its distance from the nearer tip once, then build a single hollow wing string directly, either a lone star when the wing is only one star wide, or a star, a gap of spaces, and a star otherwise. Since both wings are always identical, that same wing string can be reused on both sides of the middle gap.
For each row, compute its distance from the nearer tip once, build a single hollow wing string, and reuse it directly on both sides of the gap.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: find the distance from the nearest tip, build one hollow wing and reuse it

codes.python:
def hollow_butterfly(n):
    total_rows = 2 * n - 1
    for r in range(1, total_rows + 1):          # r counts every row, top tip to bottom tip
        m = min(r, 2 * n - r)                     # this row's distance from the nearest tip
        wing = "*" if m == 1 else "*" + " " * (m - 2) + "*"  # a hollow wing, reused on both sides
        gap = 2 * (n - m)
        row = wing + " " * gap + wing               # both wings and the gap, built directly
        print(row)                               # one print call per row instead of per character


if __name__ == "__main__":
    hollow_butterfly(4)

blocks.text: This works because m, exactly as with the solid butterfly, correctly measures every row's distance from the nearer tip and determines the width of each wing, and because that same m is used for both the left and right wing, the two are always guaranteed to be identical strings; building one hollow wing, either a single star or a star-gap-star construction, and placing it directly on both sides of the gap produces the correct row, with the special width 1 or 2 case naturally avoiding any attempt to hollow out an interior that does not exist.

items: m is computed once per row as the minimum of r and 2n minus r, exactly the same distance measurement already used for the solid butterfly.

A single hollow wing string is built from m, either a lone star or a star-gap-star construction, reusing the hollow pyramid's ordinary-row logic but applied to a wing of width m instead of a full pyramid row.
That one wing string is placed on both sides of the gap by simple concatenation, wing plus gap plus the same wing again, rather than being derived twice.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with no per cell branching and only O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared) checks.
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

codes.python:
def hollow_butterfly(n):
    total_rows = 2 * n - 1
    rows = []
    for r in range(1, total_rows + 1):
        m = min(r, 2 * n - r)
        wing = "*" if m == 1 else "*" + " " * (m - 2) + "*"
        gap = 2 * (n - m)
        rows.append(wing + " " * gap + wing)         # build every row directly, one operation each
    print("\n".join(rows))                        # join every row and output the whole pattern at once


if __name__ == "__main__":
    hollow_butterfly(4)

items: Every row is still built from its own m and single reused wing string, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is collecting each finished row instead of printing it immediately.
Joining all 2n minus 1 rows with newline characters assembles the complete hollow butterfly as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole shape, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: This shape combines the hollow, edge only region idea from the hollow pyramid with the two-wings-and-a-gap structure from the butterfly. Recognizing that both wings are always identical to each other is what allows one hollow wing string to be built once and reused, rather than being derived separately for each side.

items: Forgetting that a wing of width 1 or 2 has no interior to hollow out, and would produce an empty or incorrect string if the general formula is applied blindly.
Building the left and right wings as if they were different shapes, when they are always exactly the same string.
Getting the gap formula wrong, it should be 2 times n minus m, the same as the solid butterfly.

blocks.text: Explicitly noting which earlier idea each part of a new shape borrows from, here the hollow edge rule from one problem and the two-wing structure from another, shows a clear ability to decompose an unfamiliar shape into pieces that have already been solved.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "are the two wings really different", think: no, they are always identical for a given row, build one and reuse it.
If the interviewer says "how is this related to the hollow pyramid", think: the same edge only construction, just applied to a wing of width m instead of a full pyramid row.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: per cell wing and edge checks in the brute force version, one hollow wing built once and reused per row in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing that combines the hollow, edge only region idea from the hollow pyramid with the distance-based two-wing structure from the butterfly, plus a new insight, both wings are always identical, so only one ever needs to be built.

Core Idea: compute m, a row's distance from the nearer tip, exactly as with the butterfly, build a single hollow wing string from it, either a lone star or a star-gap-star construction, then reuse that exact same string on both sides of the gap.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: when two regions in the same row are always identical to each other, build one and reuse it rather than deriving both separately.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape by adapting the butterfly; explicitly noting the wing-reuse opportunity is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: hollow pyramid's edge rule applied to a wing, butterfly's distance measurement, build one wing and reuse it twice.
